name: A web page of 14 kB often loads noticeably faster than one of 15 kB, while the difference between 13 kB and 14 kB (or 15 kB and 16 kB) is negligible. Explain why, and show the calculation. Assume a typical initial TCP window of 10 packets, 1500-byte packets with a 40-byte header, and a round-trip time of 200 ms (100 ms each way).
answer:
The reason is TCP slow start, the algorithm TCP uses to detect the available bandwidth, i.e. how many packets it may send at a time. A typical initial window is 10 packets (settings vary, but 10 is a small and safe amount). A 1500-byte packet with a 40-byte header carries \(1500-40=1460\) bytes of data, so the first round carries \(10\cdot 1460=14\,600\) bytes, about 14 kB.

For the first 10 packets only latency matters (milliseconds in a LAN, tens of ms over wire or fibre, hundreds of ms over satellite, plus queuing in servers and routers). The 11th packet (the 15th kB) cannot be sent until the client has received the first ten and returned an ACK; only then does the server send the next, larger round (e.g. 20 packets), and it keeps growing until packets are lost or ACKs stop arriving, when it reduces the window.

So the RTT becomes significant for the 15th kB: first round 100 ms + ACK 100 ms + next round 100 ms = 300 ms, instead of about 100 ms for a page that fits into the first round. 13 vs 14 kB (both fit in round one) or 15 vs 16 kB (both need round two) differ only marginally. The TCP and TLS handshakes add further RTTs.
keyPoints: Cause: TCP slow start limits how many packets may be sent before an ACK returns
Typical initial window 10 packets; 1500 − 40 = 1460 B data each; 10 × 1460 = 14 600 B ≈ 14 kB
Data within the first round: only latency matters
Byte 14 601+ waits for the ACK of the first round: an extra RTT (100 + 100 + 100 = 300 ms)
After each acknowledged round the window grows (e.g. 20 packets) until loss or missing ACK, then it is reduced
TCP and TLS handshakes add further RTTs
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 4-6 (PDF pages 4-7)

name: State what a protocol for reliable data transmission must provide, explain why traditional TCP is considered insufficient for current networks, and name the three problems a new transport protocol has to solve.
answer:
A reliable transport protocol must ensure reliability of the transfer (retransmission of lost packets) and protection from congestion, both of the network and of the receiver.

Traditional TCP (Tahoe/Reno) is too slow for current networks with high capacity and high latency: its window grows slowly and shrinks sharply, so on such paths it cannot fill the pipe. Hence the need to go beyond Tahoe and Reno.

A new protocol must solve three problems: (1) achieve better network utilisation; (2) ensure reasonable co-existence with traditional TCP, so it does not starve ordinary users; (3) ensure gradual deployment, i.e. it must be usable while old and new protocols coexist.
keyPoints: Reliable transport = reliability (retransmissions) + congestion protection of network and receiver
Traditional TCP is too slow on high-capacity, high-latency paths
Problem 1: better utilisation
Problem 2: co-existence with traditional TCP
Problem 3: gradual deployment
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 7 and 53 (PDF pages 8 and 54)

name: Distinguish flow control from congestion control in TCP. Whom does each protect and how exact is each? Illustrate the difference with a water analogy: a tap feeds water through a pipe network into a bucket. Compare (i) a small bucket fed through a wide pipe and (ii) a large bucket fed through a network with a narrow section. Finally, explain why the Internet needed congestion control in addition to flow control.
answer:
Flow control manages the transmission rate so that a slower receiver is not overwhelmed; it is deterministic because the receiver tells the sender how much it can accept. Congestion control avoids congestion inside the network; it is only approximate, because the sender must infer the network state (from losses, delays, marks). Flow control is for receivers, congestion control for the network.

Analogy: (i) a wide pipe into a small bucket – the receiver is the bottleneck and overflows: a flow-control problem. (ii) a large bucket behind a network with a narrow section – water backs up inside the network (internal congestion) although the receiver could take much more: a congestion-control problem. In both cases the tap (sending rate) must be turned down, but for different reasons.

Why both: with flow control alone, senders keep pushing data into a saturated network, queues overflow, packets are dropped and retransmitted, and useful throughput collapses (congestion collapse). This observed collapse is what led to adding congestion control to TCP (Tahoe).
keyPoints: Flow control protects a slow receiver and is deterministic
Congestion control protects the network and is approximate (inferred)
Small bucket = receiver bottleneck (flow control); narrow network with big receiver = internal congestion
Both work by adjusting the sender's rate, but for different reasons
Without congestion control the network can suffer congestion collapse; this motivated congestion control in TCP
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 9-10 (PDF pages 10-11); the explanation of why flow control alone leads to collapse is derived

name: Define MSS, cwnd, rwnd, ownd and ssthresh as used in TCP congestion and flow control. Which side maintains or advertises each value, and how do they combine into the amount of data the sender may actually have outstanding?
answer: MSS – maximum segment size, derived from the MTU. cwnd – congestion window: kept on the sender side, adjusted dynamically by congestion control; how much data may be sent with respect to the network. rwnd – receive window: advertised by the receiver; how much data it can accept (flow control). The sender uses \[\text{ownd}=\min\{\text{cwnd},\,\text{rwnd}\}\] as the window actually used, so it respects both the network and the receiver. ssthresh – slow-start threshold: a threshold of cwnd marking the switch from slow start to congestion avoidance, i.e. from exponential to linear growth. (The slides spell it "sstresh".)
keyPoints: MSS = maximum segment size, derived from MTU
cwnd = sender-side congestion window, adjusted dynamically
rwnd = receive window advertised by the receiver
\(\text{ownd}=\min\{\text{cwnd},\text{rwnd}\}\) is the window actually used
ssthresh = cwnd threshold for switching from exponential to linear growth
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slide 9 (PDF page 10)

name: Explain TCP flow control with a sliding window. Which fields of the TCP header are used by the sender and by the receiver, and into which four regions do they divide the sender's byte stream?
answer: The sender stamps each sent segment with a Sequence Number. In the segments coming back, the receiver's Acknowledgment field says up to which byte data have been received, and its Window field advertises how much more data it is willing to accept (rwnd). On the sender's byte stream this gives four regions: acknowledged (up to the acknowledgment number – delivered and confirmed); sent but not yet acknowledged (from the acknowledgment number up to the highest sequence number sent); to be sent – data the window allows to be sent now (up to acknowledgment + advertised window); and outside the window – data the application has already written but that may not be sent until further acknowledgments or a larger window arrive. As acknowledgments arrive, the window slides forward.
keyPoints: Sender uses the Sequence Number of sent segments
Receiver returns the Acknowledgment number and the advertised Window
Regions: acknowledged | sent (unacknowledged) | to be sent (inside window) | outside window
Right edge of usable window = acknowledgment + advertised window
Window slides as acknowledgments arrive; application writes beyond it must wait
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slide 11 (PDF page 12); region boundaries read from the slide figure

name: Describe congestion control in TCP Tahoe: its components, the slow-start and congestion-avoidance phases with their per-ACK growth rules, the condition for moving between the phases, and the reaction to loss. Why is the scheme called AIMD?
answer:
Traditional congestion control is based on AIMD – Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease. Tahoe = Slow Start + AIMD + Fast Retransmit.

Connection opening: \(\text{cwnd}=1\) segment, phase Slow Start – exponential growth: for every useful acknowledgment \(\text{cwnd}\leftarrow\text{cwnd}+1\) segment, so cwnd doubles each RTT, until \(\text{cwnd}=\text{ssthresh}\).
Congestion Avoidance (from \(\text{cwnd}=\text{ssthresh}\)) – additive growth: per acknowledgment \[\text{cwnd}\leftarrow\text{cwnd}+\frac{\text{MSS}\cdot\text{MSS}}{\text{cwnd}},\] so a full window of ACKs adds one segment: \(+1\) segment per RTT without loss.
Loss (e.g. retransmission timeout, from either phase): \(\text{ssthresh}=0.5\cdot\text{cwnd}\), \(\text{cwnd}=1\) segment, back to Slow Start. Fast Retransmit is the loss detection algorithm triggered by 3 duplicate ACKs; in Tahoe it also resets cwnd.

The increase is additive (\(+1\) per RTT), the decrease multiplicative (threshold halved, window restarted) – hence AIMD.
keyPoints: Tahoe = Slow Start + AIMD + Fast Retransmit
Start \(\text{cwnd}=1\); slow start: +1 segment per ACK (doubling per RTT) until ssthresh
Congestion avoidance: \(+\text{MSS}^2/\text{cwnd}\) per ACK = +1 segment per RTT
Loss: \(\text{ssthresh}=\text{cwnd}/2\), \(\text{cwnd}=1\), return to slow start
Fast Retransmit detects loss by 3 duplicate ACKs; in Tahoe it resets cwnd
AIMD: additive increase, multiplicative decrease
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 12-13 (PDF pages 13-14)

name: A TCP connection starts with \(\text{cwnd}=1\) MSS and \(\text{ssthresh}=16\) MSS. Slow start doubles cwnd every RTT and ends exactly at ssthresh; in congestion avoidance cwnd grows by 1 MSS per RTT. In the RTT in which cwnd reaches 26 MSS, a single loss is detected by three duplicate ACKs (no timeout). Give the cwnd values, once per RTT, (a) before the loss, (b) after the loss for TCP Tahoe and (c) after the loss for TCP Reno, each until cwnd is 26 again (for Reno, ignore the temporary window inflation in Fast Recovery). How many RTTs does each need to get back to 26, and what is the average cwnd over that period? Explain the resulting long-term sawtooth shapes.
answer:
(a) Before the loss: slow start 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 (ends exactly at \(\text{ssthresh}=16\)), then congestion avoidance 17, 18, …, 26. The loss is detected at 26.
(b) Tahoe: \(\text{ssthresh}=0.5\cdot 26=13\), \(\text{cwnd}=1\). Slow start again: 1, 2, 4, 8, then, because doubling to 16 would pass the threshold, slow start ends exactly at \(\text{ssthresh}=13\) (13), and linear growth 14, 15, …, 26. That is 17 RTTs from 1 to 26; the window sizes before returning to 26 sum to \(1+2+4+8+(13+14+\dots+25)=15+247=262\), so the average is \(262/17\approx 15.4\).
(c) Reno (Fast Recovery, slow start not used): \(\text{ssthresh}=\text{cwnd}=0.5\cdot 26=13\), then 13, 14, …, 26: 13 RTTs; sum \(13+\dots+25=247\), average \(247/13=19\).

Shapes: Tahoe's sawtooth falls to 1 after every loss, rises exponentially below \(\text{ssthresh}\) and linearly above it. Reno oscillates between about \(W/2\) and \(W\) (13 and 26), recovers 4 RTTs sooner, and its average window (and throughput) is higher.
keyPoints: Before loss: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 then 17 … 26
Tahoe: ssthresh = 13, cwnd = 1, slow start 1, 2, 4, 8, 13, then linear to 26 (17 RTTs, average about 15.4)
Reno after 3 duplicate ACKs: ssthresh = cwnd = 13, linear 13 … 26 (13 RTTs, average 19)
Tahoe sawtooth falls to 1 each loss; Reno oscillates between W/2 and W
Reno keeps a higher average window and throughput
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 12-17 (PDF pages 13-18); the traces follow the Tahoe/Reno rules on slides 12-16 (the slide charts double from 8 to 16 past ssthresh = 13, a simplification); averages are derived

name: Explain Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery in TCP Reno. When are duplicate ACKs generated and how is a loss recognised? Describe the state transitions between Slow Start, Congestion Avoidance and Fast Recovery after three duplicate ACKs, after a retransmission timeout, and when the expected ACK finally arrives.
answer:
Reno = Tahoe + Fast Recovery.
Fast Retransmit: a receiver sends an immediate duplicate ACK whenever an out-of-order segment arrives, so every segment after a dropped one triggers a duplicate ACK. A loss is indicated by 3 duplicate ACKs (about four identical ACKs without intervening packets). TCP then retransmits the segment without waiting for the retransmission timer.
Fast Recovery: the slow-start phase is not used after such a loss; \(\text{ssthresh}=\text{cwnd}=0.5\cdot\text{cwnd}\).

State machine: Slow Start moves to Congestion Avoidance when \(\text{cwnd}=\text{ssthresh}\). From Slow Start or Congestion Avoidance, 3 duplicate ACKs lead to Fast Recovery, where the window is temporarily increased (“exponential increase beyond cwnd”) while waiting for the retransmitted segment to be acknowledged. When the expected ACK arrives, \(\text{cwnd}=\text{cwnd}/2\) and the connection continues in Congestion Avoidance (linear growth). A retransmission timeout – from any state – sets \(\text{ssthresh}=\text{cwnd}/2\) and returns to Slow Start with \(\text{cwnd}=1\) segment in every case.
So a mild loss signal (duplicate ACKs, data still flowing) halves the window, while a timeout (the severe signal) restarts from slow start.
keyPoints: Receiver sends an immediate duplicate ACK for every out-of-order segment
3 duplicate ACKs signal a loss; retransmit without waiting for the timer
Fast Recovery: no slow start; \(\text{ssthresh}=\text{cwnd}=\text{cwnd}/2\); window temporarily inflated
Expected ACK received: continue in Congestion Avoidance with linear growth
Timeout from any state: \(\text{ssthresh}=\text{cwnd}/2\) and back to Slow Start
Duplicate ACKs = mild signal (halve), timeout = severe signal (restart)
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 15-16 (PDF pages 16-17); the mild/severe-signal remark is an interpretation

name: Compare what TCP Tahoe, Reno, NewReno and TCP with Selective Acknowledgement (SACK) retransmit after a packet loss and how NewReno differs from Reno. Which fundamental question about traditional TCP remains open even with the best of these mechanisms?
answer:
The reaction to packet loss is retransmission: Tahoe retransmits the whole actual window (ownd); Reno retransmits a single segment in Fast Retransmission mode; NewReno is a more fine-grained variant that uses partial ACKs and handles multiple losses in one window, so it retransmits several segments; SACK retransmits just the lost packets.

The fundamental question remains: how can a sufficient cwnd be reached under real conditions on a network with high capacity and high RTT, without affecting or preventing “common” users from using the network? Better retransmission does not remove the slow additive growth of the window.
keyPoints: Tahoe: whole window
Reno: one segment per fast retransmission
NewReno: partial ACKs, several losses in one window
SACK: only the lost packets
Open: reaching a large cwnd on high-capacity, high-RTT paths without harming others; retransmission is not the bottleneck
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 15 and 19 (PDF pages 16 and 20)

name: Explain delay-based congestion control as used by TCP Vegas and FAST TCP. What signal do they use instead of (or in addition to) packet loss, how does each adjust its sending rate, and how does FAST TCP differ from Vegas?
answer:
TCP Vegas is an alternative concept of congestion control: when a network is congested, the RTT becomes higher (packets wait in queues). Vegas monitors the RTT during the transmission and when an RTT increase is detected, the congestion window is linearly reduced. It also offers a possibility to measure the available bandwidth using inter-packet spacing/dispersion.
FAST (Fast AQM Scalable TCP) uses end-to-end delay, ECN and packet losses for congestion detection/avoidance: if too few packets are queued in the routers (detected by RTT monitoring), the sending rate is increased. Differences from Vegas: Vegas makes fixed-size adjustments to the rate, independent of how far the current rate is from the target; FAST makes larger steps when the system is far from equilibrium and smaller steps near equilibrium. If ECN is available, FAST can use ECN marking to replace/supplement queueing delay and loss as the congestion measure.
keyPoints: Congestion raises RTT because of queuing
Vegas: monitors RTT, linearly reduces the window on RTT increase
Vegas: bandwidth estimate from inter-packet dispersion
FAST: uses delay, ECN and loss; increases rate when few packets are queued
Vegas fixed-size steps vs FAST step size proportional to distance from equilibrium
FAST can use ECN marks instead of / in addition to delay and loss
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 18 and 46 (PDF pages 19 and 47)

name: Define aggressiveness, responsiveness and fairness of a TCP congestion-control algorithm. What is the trade-off between high and low aggressiveness, what does fairness mean (and not mean), and why does the speed of convergence matter?
answer:
Aggressiveness: a highly aggressive TCP increases cwnd quickly or reduces it relatively little when congestion occurs; a less aggressive TCP increases cwnd more slowly or reduces it more sharply. Highly aggressive algorithms are unfair to other users, because they take up available bandwidth quickly.
Responsiveness describes how quickly and effectively TCP reacts when network conditions change: a highly responsive connection detects congestion and reduces its sending rate quickly; a less responsive one reacts more slowly, potentially causing more packet loss and delays.
Fairness: competing flows sharing a bottleneck link receive reasonable shares of its capacity. The goal is not necessarily equal throughput in every situation – RTT, priorities and application requirements differ, and flows facing different conditions may receive unequal rates. Fairness is not guaranteed – TCP is unfair. The speed of convergence to the point of equilibrium does matter: a protocol that converges slowly can leave flows unfairly treated for a long time.
keyPoints: High aggressiveness: fast increase / mild decrease; grabs bandwidth, unfair to others
Low aggressiveness: slow increase / sharp decrease
Responsiveness: how quickly the sender reacts to congestion; slow reaction means more loss and delay
Fairness: reasonable (not necessarily equal) shares of a bottleneck
TCP fairness is not guaranteed
Convergence speed to equilibrium matters
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 20-21 (PDF pages 21-22)

name: Two AIMD flows share a bottleneck of capacity 100 (arbitrary units). Plot their rates \(x\) and \(y\) as a point in a plane: the line \(x=y\) is the fairness line and \(x+y=100\) is full utilisation. Both flows add 1 unit per step (additive increase), and whenever \(x+y\) reaches 100 a loss occurs and both rates are multiplied by \(\beta\). Start at \(x=80,\ y=0\). (a) How does the operating point move during increase and during decrease, and what happens to the difference \(x-y\)? (b) Give the difference after the \(k\)-th loss. (c) How many loss cycles are needed until the difference drops below 1 for \(\beta=0.5\) and for \(\beta=0.83\)? What does the comparison say about aggressiveness and fairness?
answer:
(a) Additive increase adds the same amount to both rates, so the point moves at 45°, parallel to the fairness line, and the difference \(x-y\) stays unchanged until the sum reaches the capacity line (loss). Multiplicative decrease multiplies both rates by \(\beta\): the point jumps towards the origin along the line through it, and the difference becomes \(\beta\,(x-y)\). The trajectory therefore zig-zags between the capacity line \(x+y=100\) and the decreased line \(x+y=100\beta\), moving towards the fairness line \(x=y\).
(b) The initial difference is 80, and each loss multiplies it by \(\beta\): \[d_k=80\,\beta^{k}.\]
(c) We need \(80\beta^k<1\), i.e. \(k>\ln 80/(-\ln\beta)\).
\(\beta=0.5\): \(k>4.382/0.693=6.32\Rightarrow k=7\) (\(80\cdot0.5^7=0.625\), while \(k=6\) gives 1.25).
\(\beta=0.83\): \(k>4.382/0.1863=23.5\Rightarrow k=24\) (\(80\cdot0.83^{24}\approx0.91\), while \(k=23\) gives \(\approx1.10\)).
With a gentler decrease the unfairness shrinks only by 17 % per loss, so more than three times as many loss cycles are needed. (The cycles are shorter: the sum must regrow by \(100(1-\beta)\) at 2 units per step, i.e. 25 steps for \(\beta=0.5\) but 8.5 steps for \(\beta=0.83\).) A gentler decrease means a more aggressive, less responsive flow: higher utilisation between losses but slower convergence to fairness.
keyPoints: Additive increase moves parallel to the fairness line; difference unchanged
Multiplicative decrease scales both rates; difference multiplied by \(\beta\)
Difference after the k-th loss: \(80\beta^k\); zig-zag towards \(x=y\) on the capacity line
\(\beta=0.5\): 7 losses to get below 1; \(\beta=0.83\): 24 losses
Gentler decrease = higher utilisation but slower convergence to fairness
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 21-23 (PDF pages 22-24, simulations with additive step 1 MSS and decrease factors 0.5 and 0.83); the geometric argument and the loss-cycle counts are derived

name: Describe Scalable TCP: its update rule per RTT, per ACK and per loss, and why it is called MIMD rather than AIMD. When does it fall back to AIMD? Explain why two competing pure-MIMD flows do not converge to a fair share, in contrast to AIMD.
answer:
Scalable TCP (Tom Kelly, 2003): \(\text{cwnd}\leftarrow\text{cwnd}+0.01\,\text{cwnd}\) per RTT without loss, which is \(\text{cwnd}\leftarrow\text{cwnd}+0.01\) per ACK (a window of ACKs arrives per RTT), and \(\text{cwnd}\leftarrow0.875\,\text{cwnd}\) per packet loss. Both increase and decrease are proportional to the window ⇒ Multiplicative Increase Multiplicative Decrease (MIMD). For small windows and/or higher loss rates it switches into AIMD mode so that it stays friendly to standard TCP.

Fairness: let two flows have windows \(x\) and \(y\). A multiplicative increase by 1.01 and a decrease by 0.875 scale both windows by the same factor, so the ratio \(x/y\) is preserved; an initial imbalance is never corrected. In AIMD the additive increase keeps the difference and the multiplicative decrease shrinks it each loss, which pushes the flows towards equality.
keyPoints: Per RTT +1 % of cwnd (per ACK +0.01); per loss ×0.875
MIMD: increase and decrease both proportional to cwnd
Falls back to AIMD for small windows / high loss rates
Pure MIMD preserves the ratio of two flows: no convergence to fairness
AIMD decrease shrinks the difference between flows each loss
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 25 and 27 (PDF pages 26 and 28); the ratio argument interprets the fairness simulation on slide 27 and is derived

name: A path can hold \(c=1000\) packets per RTT (its bandwidth-delay product expressed in packets) and \(\text{RTT}=100\) ms. After a loss at full rate, standard TCP halves its window to \(c/2\) and then grows by 1 packet per RTT. Scalable TCP reduces the window to \(0.875\,c\) and then grows by a factor 1.01 per RTT. Compute how long each needs to get back to \(c\). Then repeat for a ten times faster path (\(c=10\,000\) packets per RTT) and explain which quantity the recovery time depends on in each protocol.
answer:
Standard TCP: from \(c/2=500\) to \(1000\) at +1 per RTT: \(c/2=500\) RTT \(=500\cdot0.1\text{ s}=\mathbf{50\ s}\). For \(c=10\,000\): 5000 RTT = 500 s.
Scalable TCP: from \(0.875c\) we need \(0.875\,c\cdot1.01^{n}\ge c\), i.e. \[n=\frac{\ln(1/0.875)}{\ln 1.01}=\frac{0.1335}{0.00995}\approx 13.4\ \text{RTT}\approx\mathbf{1.34\ s}.\] For \(c=10\,000\) the result is the same, about 13.4 RTT.

Standard TCP's recovery time grows with cwnd (capacity) and RTT, so it becomes unusable on fast long-distance links. Scalable TCP's recovery time depends only on the RTT (and the constants 0.875 and 1.01), not on the window size.
keyPoints: Standard TCP: \(c/2\) RTT = 500 RTT = 50 s; 500 s at ten times the capacity
Scalable TCP: \(\ln(1/0.875)/\ln 1.01\approx13.4\) RTT \(\approx1.34\) s, same for any c
Standard recovery time proportional to cwnd and RTT
Scalable recovery time proportional to RTT only
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 25-26 (PDF pages 26-27); the numeric example applies the recovery-time expressions of slide 26 and the c = 10 000 case is derived

name: What is a response curve (response function) of a TCP variant? Explain what the curves of standard TCP, HighSpeed TCP (HSTCP) and Scalable TCP mean for (a) fast links with very low loss rates and (b) congested links with high loss rates. Use these data: HSTCP sustains about 38 packets/RTT (the same as standard TCP) at loss rate \(p=10^{-3}\) and about 83 000 packets/RTT at \(p=10^{-7}\). For standard TCP use the approximation \(w\approx 1.2/\sqrt{p}\). How many times larger is HSTCP's window at \(p=10^{-7}\), and what bit rate does that window correspond to with 1500-byte packets and \(\text{RTT}=100\) ms?
answer:
A response curve plots the window (sending rate in packets/RTT) a TCP variant sustains as a function of the packet loss rate, on log–log axes. Standard TCP has the flattest curve; HSTCP and Scalable TCP are steeper at low loss.
(a) Low loss rates: the new variants sustain far larger windows than standard TCP, which is what a fast long-distance link needs. (b) High loss rates: HSTCP coincides with standard TCP for \(p\ge10^{-3}\) (about 38 packets/RTT) and Scalable TCP also switches to AIMD for small windows/higher loss, so both stay friendly to standard TCP on congested links.

Computation: standard TCP at \(p=10^{-3}\): \(1.2/\sqrt{10^{-3}}=1.2/0.0316\approx38\) (agrees with HSTCP). At \(p=10^{-7}\): \(1.2/\sqrt{10^{-7}}=1.2/(3.16\cdot10^{-4})\approx3800\) packets/RTT. HSTCP: \(83\,000/3800\approx\mathbf{22}\) times larger. Rate: \(83\,000\cdot1500\cdot8\approx9.96\cdot10^{8}\) bit per RTT, divided by 0.1 s gives about \(\mathbf{10\ Gb/s}\), whereas standard TCP would reach only about 0.46 Gb/s (\(3800\cdot12\,000/0.1\approx4.6\cdot10^8\) b/s).
keyPoints: Response curve: sustained window/rate versus loss rate (log–log)
Low loss: HSTCP/Scalable sustain much larger windows (needed on fast long-distance links)
High loss (\(p\ge10^{-3}\)): HSTCP equals standard TCP, Scalable uses AIMD: friendliness
Standard TCP \(w\approx1.2/\sqrt p\): 38 at \(10^{-3}\), about 3800 at \(10^{-7}\)
HSTCP window at \(10^{-7}\) is about 22 times larger, about 10 Gb/s at 100 ms RTT
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 28-29 and 32 (PDF pages 29-30 and 33), values read from the response-curve charts; the standard-TCP approximation w = 1.2/sqrt(p) and the rate computation are general knowledge/derived

name: Describe HighSpeed TCP (HSTCP, RFC 3649): how its increase and decrease rules depend on the window, how it behaves for small and for large windows, how it relates to Scalable TCP and to multi-stream TCP, and which limitation it shares with Scalable TCP.
answer:
HSTCP (Sally Floyd, RFC 3649) is an AIMD/MIMD scheme whose parameters depend on the current window: \(\text{cwnd}\leftarrow\text{cwnd}+a(\text{cwnd})\) per RTT without loss (\(+a(\text{cwnd})/\text{cwnd}\) per ACK), and on a loss the window is decreased by a window-dependent factor \(b(\text{cwnd})\).
For small windows and/or high loss rates it emulates traditional TCP (halving, +1 per RTT); for large windows it increases faster and decreases less, so it can fill high-capacity paths.
A parametrisation equivalent to Scalable TCP is possible (Linear HSTCP). Compared with multi-stream TCP: the number of parallel standard TCP connections that the HSTCP response function emulates at window \(\text{cwnd}\) is \(N(\text{cwnd})\approx0.23\,\text{cwnd}^{0.4}\), so HSTCP behaves like a bundle of standard connections that grows with the window.
Shared limitation: neither Scalable TCP nor HSTCP deals with the slow-start phase.
keyPoints: Window-dependent increase \(a(\text{cwnd})\) and decrease \(b(\text{cwnd})\)
Emulates traditional TCP for small windows / high loss; faster increase and smaller decrease for large windows
Linear HSTCP is equivalent to Scalable TCP
Equivalent to \(N(\text{cwnd})\) parallel standard TCP connections
Neither HSTCP nor Scalable TCP improves slow start
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 29-32 (PDF pages 30-33)

name: HighSpeed TCP decreases its window after a loss by the fraction \(b(w)=-\dfrac{0.4\,(\ln w-3.64)}{7.69}+0.5\) (natural logarithm, \(w\) in MSS) and emulates \(N(w)\approx0.23\,w^{0.4}\) parallel standard TCP connections. Compute \(b\) and \(N\) for \(w=38\), \(w=10\,000\) and \(w=83\,000\). What window does a loss at \(w=10\,000\) leave, compared with standard TCP, and what do the results say about the design?
answer:
\(w=38\): \(\ln38=3.64\), so \(b=0.5\) (standard halving) and \(N=0.23\cdot38^{0.4}=0.23\cdot4.29\approx1\) connection, i.e. standard TCP.
\(w=10\,000\): \(\ln w=9.21\), \(b=-0.4\cdot(9.21-3.64)/7.69+0.5=-0.29+0.5\approx0.21\); \(N=0.23\cdot10\,000^{0.4}=0.23\cdot10^{1.6}=0.23\cdot39.8\approx9\) connections. A loss removes 21 % of the window: it falls to about \(10\,000\cdot0.79\approx7900\), while standard TCP would halve it to 5000.
\(w=83\,000\): \(\ln w=11.33\), \(b=-0.4\cdot7.69/7.69+0.5\approx0.1\); \(N=0.23\cdot83\,000^{0.4}\approx0.23\cdot92.8\approx21\) connections.
So the decrease fraction slides from 0.5 at small windows to 0.1 at very large ones while the emulated number of connections grows: at small windows HSTCP is just standard TCP, at huge windows it is much more aggressive and backs off only gently.
keyPoints: \(w=38\): \(b=0.5\), \(N\approx1\) – equal to standard TCP
\(w=10\,000\): \(b\approx0.21\), \(N\approx9\); window falls to about 7900 (standard TCP: 5000)
Decrease fraction shrinks and emulated connection count grows with the window
Small windows behave as standard TCP; very large windows are more aggressive
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 30-32 (PDF pages 31-33); the numerical evaluation is derived; RFC 3649 defines b as the fraction by which the window is reduced, whereas the slide writes cwnd = b(cwnd)·cwnd, and the natural logarithm is inferred from b(38) = 0.5 and b(83 000) = 0.1

name: Explain the idea of H-TCP. On what does its increase rate depend and why, what does it keep from standard TCP, and how does it choose the decrease factor? Describe the roles of \(\Delta\), \(\Delta_L\), \(\Delta_B\), \(T_{\min}\), \(T_{\max}\) and \(B(k)\).
answer:
H-TCP (Hamilton Institute, Ireland) makes a simple change to the cwnd increase function: its aggressiveness (the additive-increase rate \(\alpha\)) grows with the time since the last loss (backoff). Shortly after a loss it behaves like standard TCP; the longer the connection has run without loss, the faster it increases, so it can fill a high-capacity path. The AIMD mechanism is kept, and it preserves many key properties of standard TCP: fairness, responsiveness and the relationship to buffering.

Quantities: \(\Delta\) – time elapsed since the last congestion; \(\Delta_L\) – for \(\Delta\le\Delta_L\) standard TCP growth is used; \(\Delta_B\) – threshold on the relative throughput change above which the standard 0.5 decrease is used (significant bandwidth change); \(T_{\min},T_{\max}\) – minimal and maximal measured RTT; \(B(k)\) – maximum throughput measured in the last interval without loss.
Decrease: after a significant throughput change use 0.5; otherwise use \(\min\{T_{\min}/T_{\max},\,0.8\}\) – a mild decrease when RTT variation (queueing) is small.
keyPoints: Increase rate grows with the time since the last backoff; AIMD is kept
For \(\Delta\le\Delta_L\) standard TCP growth
Decrease factor: 0.5 after a significant throughput change, otherwise \(\min\{T_{\min}/T_{\max},0.8\}\)
\(T_{\min},T_{\max}\): min/max RTT; \(B(k)\): max throughput in last loss-free interval
Preserves fairness, responsiveness, relation to buffering
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 33-35 (PDF pages 34-36); the interpretation of the RTT ratio as a queueing indicator is derived

name: H-TCP uses the quadratic increment \(a'(\Delta)=1+10(\Delta-\Delta_L)+0.5(\Delta-\Delta_L)^2\) (\(\Delta\) in seconds) once \(\Delta>\Delta_L\), and the decrease factor (the window is multiplied by \(b\) after a loss) \(b(B)=0.5\) if the relative throughput change \(\left|\dfrac{B(k+1)-B(k)}{B(k)}\right|\) exceeds \(\Delta_B\), otherwise \(b(B)=\min\{T_{\min}/T_{\max},\,0.8\}\). Compute \(a'\) for \(\Delta-\Delta_L=0,\ 2\) and \(10\) s, and \(b\) for (i) \(T_{\min}=60\) ms, \(T_{\max}=100\) ms with an insignificant throughput change, (ii) \(T_{\min}=90\) ms, \(T_{\max}=100\) ms with an insignificant change, (iii) a significant throughput change. Interpret the results.
answer:
Increment: \(\Delta-\Delta_L=0\): \(a'=1\). \(\Delta-\Delta_L=2\): \(1+20+0.5\cdot4=\mathbf{23}\). \(\Delta-\Delta_L=10\): \(1+100+0.5\cdot100=\mathbf{151}\). The increase grows quadratically with the time since the loss: right after a loss H-TCP is as gentle as standard TCP, after a long loss-free period it is very aggressive.
Decrease: (i) \(\min\{60/100,0.8\}=\mathbf{0.6}\) (window reduced to 60 %); (ii) \(\min\{90/100,0.8\}=\mathbf{0.8}\) (capped, window reduced only to 80 %); (iii) \(b=\mathbf{0.5}\), the standard halving. When the RTT hardly varies (little queueing) the link is not saturated and a small decrease suffices; when throughput changes significantly (competing traffic) H-TCP backs off as standard TCP does.
keyPoints: \(a'=1\), 23 and 151 for \(\Delta-\Delta_L=0,2,10\): quadratic growth with time since loss
(iii) significant throughput change: \(b=0.5\)
Aggressive after long loss-free time, standard-like right after a loss
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 35-36 (PDF pages 35-36); the numeric evaluation and its interpretation are derived

name: Describe the four phases of BIC-TCP and explain why binary search lets the window grow quickly while it is far from the previous loss point \(W_{\max}\) but slowly when it is close to it. What benefits are claimed for BIC?
answer:
BIC-TCP (a former default in Linux) updates cwnd by a binary-search algorithm. Phases: (1) Reaction to loss – after standard multiplicative decrease it records \(W_{\max}\) (cwnd before the loss) and \(W_{\min}\) (cwnd after); since the loss occurred around \(W_{\max}\), the equilibrium is searched in \(\langle W_{\min};W_{\max}\rangle\). (2) Additive increase – jumping straight to the midpoint \((W_{\min}+W_{\max})/2\) might be too challenging for the network, so if that midpoint is more than \(S_{\max}\) above \(W_{\min}\), cwnd grows linearly by \(S_{\max}\) per RTT. (3) Binary search – cwnd jumps to the midpoint; success moves \(W_{\min}\) up, a loss moves \(W_{\max}\) down; the steps halve until they fall below \(S_{\min}\), then \(\text{cwnd}=W_{\max}\). (4) Maximum probing – the inverse process beyond \(W_{\max}\): first inverse binary search (slowly growing steps), and once the growth exceeds \(S_{\max}\), linear growth with a large fixed increment.

Why fast then slow: the midpoint step is half the remaining distance to \(W_{\max}\), so far away steps are large (capped by \(S_{\max}\) for safety), and close to \(W_{\max}\), where the last loss indicates that the capacity limit is near, the steps become tiny and the window lingers on a “plateau”.
Claimed benefits: friendliness to traditional TCP (flows can grow during the plateau; phases 2 and 4 are AIMD-like, though faster) and a more stable window, hence better utilisation, since BIC should spend most of its time near \(W_{\max}\).
keyPoints: Four phases: reaction to loss, additive increase, binary search, maximum probing
Loss: remember \(W_{\max}\) (before) and \(W_{\min}\) (after) and search between them
Additive increase by \(S_{\max}\) when the midpoint is farther than \(S_{\max}\)
Binary search halves the step: fast far from \(W_{\max}\), slow near it; stops below \(S_{\min}\)
Maximum probing beyond \(W_{\max}\): inverse binary search, then linear
Benefits: TCP friendliness on the plateau, stable window, better utilisation
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 36-39 (PDF pages 37-40); the explanation of fast-far/slow-near is derived from the midpoint rule

name: BIC-TCP rules: after a loss it sets \(W_{\max}\) (window before the loss) and \(W_{\min}\) (window after). Each RTT the target is the midpoint \((W_{\min}+W_{\max})/2\); if the midpoint is more than \(S_{\max}\) above \(W_{\min}\), the window grows only to \(W_{\min}+S_{\max}\). When a target is reached without loss, \(W_{\min}\) is set to the new window. When the step to the next target would be smaller than \(S_{\min}\), the window is set to \(W_{\max}\). Trace the window per RTT after a loss with \(W_{\max}=100\), \(W_{\min}=60\), \(S_{\max}=16\), \(S_{\min}=1\), assuming no further loss, and state which phase each step belongs to.
answer:
Step 1: midpoint \((60+100)/2=80\); \(80>60+16=76\) ⇒ additive increase: \(\text{cwnd}=60+16=\mathbf{76}\).
Target reached without loss ⇒ \(W_{\min}=76\). Step 2: midpoint 88; \(88\le76+16=92\) ⇒ binary search: \(\mathbf{88}\) (step 12). \(W_{\min}=88\): midpoint 94 ⇒ 94 (step 6); \(W_{\min}=94\): midpoint 97 ⇒ 97 (step 3); \(W_{\min}=97\): midpoint 98.5 ⇒ 98.5 (step 1.5); \(W_{\min}=98.5\): the next step would be \(99.25-98.5=0.75Trace: 76, 88, 94, 97, 98.5, 100. Growth is linear first and then logarithmic (steps 12, 6, 3, 1.5 halve). Beyond 100 the maximum-probing phase starts slowly and then becomes linear.
keyPoints: Midpoint 80 exceeds \(60+16=76\), so additive step to 76
Then binary search: 88, 94, 97, 98.5 (steps 12, 6, 3, 1.5 halve)
Next step 0.75 is below \(S_{\min}\): window set to \(W_{\max}=100\)
Linear first, then logarithmic growth
Beyond \(W_{\max}\): maximum probing
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 37-39 (PDF pages 38-40); the numeric trace applies the slide rules

name: Why was CUBIC introduced as a successor of BIC, and what is its window function? Explain the meaning of \(C\), \(T\), \(K\), \(W_{\max}\) and \(\beta\), and describe the shape of the curve: why does the window grow quickly just after a loss, slowly around \(W_{\max}\) and quickly again beyond it?
answer:
Even though BIC is quite scalable, fair and stable, its growth function is still considered too aggressive for TCP, especially under short RTTs or low-speed networks. CUBIC is a new release of BIC that uses a cubic function; for simplicity of analysis the number of phases was reduced. It is the current default in the Linux kernel.
\[W_{\text{cubic}}=C\,(T-K)^3+W_{\max},\qquad K=\sqrt[3]{\frac{W_{\max}\,\beta}{C}}\]
\(C\) is a scaling constant, \(T\) the time since the last loss event, \(W_{\max}\) the window before the loss and \(\beta\) a constant decrease factor; \(K\) is the time at which the curve returns to \(W_{\max}\).
Shape: at \(T=0\) the window is \(W_{\max}(1-\beta)\); the cubic is steep while \(|T-K|\) is large, so the window climbs quickly towards \(W_{\max}\) (concave part), flattens near \(T=K\) (the plateau around the last loss point, where the network is most likely near its limit) and then accelerates again (convex part) to probe for new bandwidth.
keyPoints: BIC still too aggressive for TCP, especially at short RTT / low speed; CUBIC has fewer phases and is the Linux default
\(W_{\text{cubic}}=C(T-K)^3+W_{\max}\), \(K=\sqrt[3]{W_{\max}\beta/C}\)
\(T\) = time since last loss; \(W_{\max}\) = window before the loss; \(\beta\) = decrease factor; \(C\) = scaling constant
Concave growth back to \(W_{\max}\), plateau at \(T\approx K\)
Convex growth beyond \(W_{\max}\) probes for more bandwidth
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slide 40 (PDF page 41); the explanation of the curve shape is derived from the formula

name: CUBIC uses \(W(T)=C\,(T-K)^3+W_{\max}\) with \(K=\sqrt[3]{W_{\max}\beta/C}\), where \(T\) is the time in seconds since the last loss. For \(W_{\max}=100\) segments, \(\beta=0.2\) and \(C=0.4\) compute \(K\), the window just after the loss (\(T=0\)), at \(T=K\) and at \(T=2K\), and interpret the values.
answer: \[K=\sqrt[3]{\frac{100\cdot0.2}{0.4}}=\sqrt[3]{50}\approx\mathbf{3.68\ s}.\]\(W(0)=0.4\cdot(-K)^3+100=-0.4\cdot50+100=\mathbf{80}\) segments, i.e. the window drops by the fraction \(\beta=0.2\). \(W(K)=100=W_{\max}\) (back at the old maximum after 3.68 s). \(W(2K)=0.4\cdot K^3+100=0.4\cdot50+100=\mathbf{120}\) segments: beyond \(W_{\max}\) the window probes for more bandwidth, ending 20 above \(W_{\max}\), mirroring the 20 below it at \(T=0\).
keyPoints: \(K=\sqrt[3]{50}\approx3.68\) s
Curve is symmetric around \((K,W_{\max})\): concave below, convex above
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slide 40 (PDF page 41); the numeric example applies the slide formula

name: Describe the Quick-Start (Limited Slow-Start) proposal. What assumption motivates it, which IP option fields does it use, and how do the sender, the routers and the receiver handle them? A sender requests an initial rate of 100 Mb/s on a path with four routers, one of which can only offer 40 Mb/s. What does the sender learn (a) if all four routers support Quick-Start and (b) if one router does not support it? What is the main drawback?
answer:
Motivation: a strong assumption that the slow-start phase cannot be improved without interaction with lower network layers. Proposal: a 4-byte option in the IP header with the fields QS TTL and Initial Rate. The sender that wants to use QS sets the QS TTL to an arbitrary (but high enough) value and the Initial Rate to the requested starting rate, and sends the SYN packet. Each router on the path that supports QS decreases the QS TTL by one and decreases the Initial Rate if necessary. The receiver returns the QS TTL and Initial Rate in the SYN/ACK. The sender knows whether all routers on the path support QS by comparing the QS TTL with the TTL, then sets the appropriate cwnd and continues with its normal congestion control (e.g. AIMD).
(a) All four routers decrement the QS TTL in step with the IP TTL and the limiting router lowers the rate: the sender learns an approved rate of 40 Mb/s and starts with a matching cwnd. (b) The QS TTL has decreased by 3 while the IP TTL decreased by 4: the mismatch shows that not all routers approved the request, so the returned rate cannot be relied on and the sender should not use it (falling back to normal slow start is an inference; the course material only says the sender learns whether all routers support QS).
Drawback: it requires changes in the IP layer (every router must support it).
keyPoints: Assumption: slow start cannot be improved without lower-layer help
4-byte IP option: QS TTL + Initial Rate, sent in the SYN
QS routers decrement QS TTL and may lower the rate; receiver echoes them in SYN/ACK
Comparing QS TTL and TTL reveals whether every router took part
Example: approved 40 Mb/s if all support; mismatch means the rate is not trustworthy
Requires IP-layer changes in routers
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 42-43 (PDF pages 43-44)

name: Explain Early Congestion Notification (ECN) and the E-TCP proposal built on it. Who sets and who mirrors the ECN bit, how should TCP react, how does E-TCP change this, and what deployment problems do both have?
answer:
ECN is a component of Active Queue Management (AQM) (the slide writes “Advanced”): a bit that is set by routers when congestion of a link/buffer/queue is coming. The ECN flag has to be mirrored by the receiver back to the sender, and TCP should react to the ECN bit in the same way as to a packet loss. Problem: it requires the routers' administrators to configure AQM/ECN.
E-TCP proposes to mirror the ECN bit just once (the first time only) and to freeze cwnd when an ACK with the ECN bit set is received from the receiver, instead of reducing it. Because of fairness, it requires introducing small (synthetic) losses into the network in order to still perform a multiplicative decrease. Problem: it requires a change in the receivers' behaviour to the ECN bit.
keyPoints: ECN: part of AQM (Active Queue Management; the slide says “Advanced”); routers set the bit when congestion is coming
Receiver mirrors the ECN flag; sender reacts as to a loss
ECN needs routers configured for AQM/ECN
E-TCP: mirror once, freeze cwnd on ECN instead of decreasing
E-TCP needs synthetic losses for fairness (multiplicative decrease)
E-TCP requires changed receiver behaviour
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 44-45 (PDF pages 45-46)

name: Explain the idea of transport approaches that split control and data into separate TCP and UDP channels, using tsunami. What does each channel carry, how are losses handled, and what does tsunami make configurable? Why can this design avoid the limits of standard TCP congestion control?
answer:
tsunami splits the communication into two streams, using TCP and UDP simultaneously. A TCP connection is an out-of-band control channel: negotiation of connection parameters, retransmission requests – it uses NACKs instead of ACKs (the receiver reports what is missing) – and negotiation of connection termination. A UDP channel carries the bulk data under MIMD congestion control, and it is highly configurable (MIMD parameters, loss threshold, maximum size of the retransmission queue, interval of sending retransmission requests, etc.).
Because reliability is handled by NACK-based retransmission requests on the control channel, the data flow is not tied to TCP's ACK-clocked AIMD window, so the data channel can use its own, more aggressive MIMD control (this reasoning is derived).
keyPoints: TCP = out-of-band control channel (negotiation, retransmission requests, termination)
UDP = data channel
NACKs instead of ACKs
UDP channel uses MIMD congestion control
Highly configurable: MIMD parameters, loss threshold, retransmission queue, request interval
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slide 48 (PDF page 49); the explanation of the avoided limits is derived

name: Describe how Reliable Blast UDP (RBUDP) transfers data. For which kind of transfers was it proposed, how is the sending rate chosen, and how does an RBUDP transfer proceed step by step until all data are delivered?
answer:
RBUDP uses an out-of-band TCP channel for control and UDP for data. It was proposed for disk-to-disk transfers, or transfers where the complete data can be held in the sender's memory. It sends at a user-defined rate; app_perf (a modified iperf that also accounts for the extra memory copy applications perform) is used to estimate the capacity of the network/receiver.
Steps: (1) the sender “blasts” the data over UDP at the predefined rate; (2) when this transmission ends, the sender sends a DONE signal over the TCP control channel; (3) the receiver answers with a mask (bitmap) of the data that arrived; (4) the sender re-sends the missing data over UDP; steps 2-4 repeat until the mask shows that all data are delivered; then the transfer ends.
keyPoints: Out-of-band TCP control channel, UDP data channel
For disk-to-disk transfers or data that fits into the sender's memory
User-defined sending rate, estimated with app_perf
Sender blasts data, then DONE over TCP; receiver returns a mask of received data
Missing data re-sent; repeat until complete
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 49-50 (PDF pages 50-51)

name: Characterise SCTP, DCCP and Reliable UDP as alternatives to TCP: what reliability, ordering and congestion control does each provide and what distinctive features? Finally, the protocol QUIC is the UDP-based design that in practice succeeded as a TCP replacement: what motivated its design?
answer:
SCTP: multi-stream (several streams in parallel, e.g. a web page and an image); multi-homed (an end node may have several IP addresses); message-oriented like UDP, but ensures reliable, in-sequence delivery of messages with congestion control like TCP.
DCCP: a non-reliable protocol with congestion control compatible with TCP.
Reliable UDP: reliable and in-order delivery up to a maximum number of retransmissions; connection parameters can be set per connection; originally for IP telephony.
QUIC is UDP-based and its design was motivated by the issues of HTTP (covered in the next lecture). Building on UDP also avoids the deployment obstacle of changing the IP layer or of new protocol numbers (derived).
keyPoints: SCTP: multi-stream, multi-homed, message-oriented, reliable in-sequence, TCP-like congestion control
DCCP: unreliable, TCP-compatible congestion control
Reliable UDP: reliable in-order up to a retransmission limit; per-connection parameters
QUIC: UDP-based replacement for TCP, motivated by HTTP issues
UDP basis eases deployment (derived)
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 51 and 54 (PDF pages 52 and 55-56); the deployment remark is derived

name: Approaches that go beyond traditional TCP can be grouped into (1) improved TCP congestion control, (2) TCP extensions with IP (lower-layer) support, (3) combinations of UDP and TCP and (4) alternative transport protocols. Name at least two examples of each group, assess how deployable each group is, and explain why interaction with lower layers (L3 or L2) is considered not very feasible.
answer:
1. Improving TCP congestion control – end-host changes only: Scalable TCP, HighSpeed TCP, H-TCP, BIC, CUBIC. They change how cwnd grows and shrinks, can be deployed gradually (CUBIC is the Linux default) and try to remain friendly to standard TCP for small windows/high loss.
2. TCP extensions with IP support: Quick-Start (IP option handled by routers), ECN/E-TCP (routers mark congestion; E-TCP also needs changed receivers and synthetic losses), FAST (delay-based, can use ECN). Judged not very feasible: they need changes in the IP layer of every router on the path, AQM/ECN configured by router administrators, or changed receiver behaviour – in conflict with gradual deployment.
3. Combining UDP and TCP: data over UDP, control over TCP – tsunami, RBUDP.
4. Alternative protocols: SCTP, Reliable UDP, DCCP; the one that succeeded in practice is QUIC (UDP-based).
The goals stay the same: aggressiveness (use bandwidth), responsiveness (recover from loss) and fairness for all users, because traditional TCP is too slow for today's networks.
keyPoints: Group 1 (Scalable, HSTCP, H-TCP, BIC, CUBIC): end hosts only, gradually deployable
Group 2 (Quick-Start, ECN/E-TCP, FAST): need router, administrator or receiver changes: not very feasible
Group 3 (tsunami, RBUDP): data over UDP, control over TCP
Group 4 (SCTP, Reliable UDP, DCCP; QUIC as the winner)
Common goals: aggressiveness, responsiveness, fairness
source: PA191 L6, lecture06.pdf, slides 43-47 and 53-54 (PDF pages 44-48 and 54-56); the deployability assessment is inferred from the requirements marked as drawbacks on slides 43-46
